title: Happy Eyeballs Version 2: Better Connectivity Using Concurrency
summary: Hostnames often resolve to several IP addresses, and some addresses or address families may be broken or slow. Happy Eyeballs version 2 lets clients try multiple connections concurrently, with short delays, so users get a working, fast connection quickly. It updates the idea from the original specification.

plainLanguage.summary: When a program connects to a server by name, the name can point to several addresses, and some of them may be broken or slow. Happy Eyeballs version 2 starts several connection attempts a short time apart and keeps the first one that works, so a user does not wait for a slow address to time out.

questions: how to choose between ipv4 and ipv6 quickly
what is the happy eyeballs resolution delay
what is the connection attempt delay in happy eyeballs
how does happy eyeballs sort addresses
how long does happy eyeballs wait between connection attempts
subtitle: Race connection attempts to IPv6 and IPv4 addresses with short delays so users get a working connection fast.

tldr.problem: A hostname often resolves to several IP addresses, and an address or a whole address family may be blocked, broken or slow, so a client that tries them one at a time leaves users waiting.
tldr.mechanism: The client sends AAAA and A queries at the same time, sorts the addresses it receives, interleaves the address families and starts connection attempts one after another with short delays, keeping the first attempt that succeeds.
tldr.outcome: The algorithm obsoletes the original description in RFC 6555 and adds DNS handling, several addresses per family, historical data and support for IPv6-only networks. Its delay values were measured on production devices and are expected to change over time.

today: RFC 8305 is a Proposed Standard published in December 2017. It obsoletes RFC 6555, and no later RFC is recorded as obsoleting or updating it. The RFC states that the approach has been deployed at scale and measured for several years.

sections.title: Why Connections to a Name Are Slow
sections.content:
Many protocols on the modern Internet use hostnames, and a hostname often resolves to several IP addresses. Each of those addresses can have different performance and connectivity characteristics. Because specific addresses, or whole address families such as IPv4 or IPv6, may be blocked, broken or sub-optimal on a network, a client that attempts multiple connections in parallel has a chance of establishing a connection more quickly.

This document specifies requirements for algorithms that reduce the delay the user sees and provides an example algorithm. The method is called the Happy Eyeballs Connection Setup. It obsoletes the original description in RFC 6555: now that the approach has been deployed at scale and measured for several years, the algorithm specification could be refined to improve its reliability and general applicability.

The algorithm has several stages, to avoid delays to the user whenever possible while preferring the use of IPv6. The document covers how to handle DNS queries when starting a connection on a dual-stack client, how to create an ordered list of destination addresses, and how to race the connection attempts.
sections.plainLanguage: A server name can point to several addresses, and on some networks one of them, or one whole kind of address, is broken or slow. Starting a single attempt and waiting for it to fail leaves the user waiting. This RFC starts several attempts a short time apart instead.

sections.title: The Four Phases
sections.content:
The RFC divides connection establishment into four phases: initiation of asynchronous DNS queries (Section 3), sorting of the resolved destination addresses (Section 4), initiation of asynchronous connection attempts (Section 5), and the establishment of one connection, which cancels all other attempts.

The document assumes that the preference policy for the host destination address favors IPv6 over IPv4. IPv6 has many desirable properties designed to be improvements over IPv4, as described in RFC 8200. If the host is configured to have a different preference, the recommendations in the document can be easily adapted.
sections.plainLanguage: Setting up a connection happens in four steps: ask for addresses, put them in order, start trying them, and stop when one works. The method prefers IPv6, and a host that prefers something else can adapt the steps.

sections.title: Asking for Addresses
sections.content:
A client with both IPv4 and IPv6 connectivity needs to send out both an AAAA and an A DNS query. Both queries SHOULD be made as soon after one another as possible, with the AAAA query made first and immediately followed by the A query.

Implementations SHOULD NOT wait for both families of answers to return before attempting connection establishment. If one query fails to return or takes significantly longer, waiting for the second address family can significantly delay a connection that the first family could have made. The client SHOULD therefore treat DNS resolution as asynchronous. If the platform has no asynchronous DNS API, the same behavior can be simulated with two separate synchronous queries on different threads, one per address family.

If a positive AAAA response, a response with at least one valid AAAA record, is received first, the first IPv6 connection attempt is immediately started. If a positive A response is received first because the answers were reordered, the client SHOULD wait a short time for the AAAA response so that preference is given to IPv6; it is common for the AAAA response to follow the A response by a few milliseconds. This wait is the Resolution Delay, and the recommended value is 50 milliseconds. A positive AAAA response within that period starts the IPv6 attempt at once. A negative AAAA response, no error and no data, or no AAAA response by the end of the period, means the client SHOULD proceed to sorting and staggered attempts using the IPv4 addresses returned so far. If the AAAA response arrives while those attempts are running, the new IPv6 addresses are added to the candidate list and the attempts continue with them.

Section 3.1 adds a rule for the DNS servers themselves. When several DNS server addresses are configured for the current network, queries SHOULD be sent over IPv6 first, meaning the address family used to carry the DNS message, not the type of query. An address that gives no response may be marked as penalized, and queries can be sent to other DNS server addresses. Client systems SHOULD NOT have an explicit limit on the number of DNS servers that can be configured; if hardware limitations require one, the client SHOULD use at least one address from each address family.
sections.plainLanguage: The client asks for both kinds of address at once, IPv6 first, and does not wait for both answers before it starts connecting. If the IPv4 answer comes back first, it waits 50 milliseconds to give IPv6 a chance. If IPv6 does not answer in that time, the client starts with the addresses it already has.

sections.title: Putting the Addresses in Order
sections.content:
Before attempting to connect, the client defines the order in which to start the attempts. The ordered list SHOULD involve all addresses from both families received by that point, so that the client gets the racing effect for the entire list and not just for the first IPv4 and first IPv6 addresses.

The client MUST sort the addresses with Destination Address Selection, from Section 6 of RFC 6724. A client that is stateful and has a history of expected round-trip times SHOULD add a Destination Address Selection rule between rules 8 and 9 that prefers addresses with lower round-trip times. A client that keeps track of the addresses it used in the past SHOULD add another rule, between the round-trip-time rule and rule 9, that prefers used addresses over unused ones. That helps servers that use the client's IP address during authentication, as in TCP Fast Open and some HTTP cookies. This historical data MUST NOT be used across different network interfaces and SHOULD be flushed whenever a device changes the network it is attached to.

The client SHOULD then interleave the address families: whichever family is first in the sorted list should be followed by an address of the other family. An implementation MAY favor one family more by allowing several addresses of that family to be attempted first, and the number of contiguous addresses of the first family is the First Address Family Count. The reason for interleaving is to avoid waiting through a long list of addresses from one family when connectivity over that family is impaired.

The address selection described here applies only to destination addresses. Source Address Selection, Section 5 of RFC 6724, is performed once per destination address and is out of scope.
sections.plainLanguage: The client sorts the addresses it has, then arranges them so that the two kinds alternate. A broken kind therefore cannot hold up the whole list. If it remembers past connections, it can also put addresses it has used before at the front.

sections.title: Racing the Connection Attempts
sections.content:
Once the list of addresses has been constructed, the client attempts connections. Connection attempts SHOULD NOT be made simultaneously, to avoid unreasonable network load. One attempt to a single address is started first, followed by the others in the list, one at a time. Starting a new attempt does not affect previous attempts, so several attempts may occur in parallel.

Once one attempt succeeds, generally when the TCP handshake completes, all other attempts that have not yet succeeded SHOULD be canceled, and any address not yet attempted SHOULD be ignored. The asynchronous DNS query MAY then be canceled, since new addresses will not be used for this connection. The DNS client resolver SHOULD still process DNS replies from the network for a short period, recommended to be 1 second, because they populate the DNS cache and can be used for subsequent connections.

The wait before the next attempt is the Connection Attempt Delay. A simple implementation uses a fixed delay, and one recommended default is 250 milliseconds. A more nuanced implementation should base its delay on the time when the previous attempt sends its second TCP SYN, following the TCP retransmission timer of RFC 6298, and should only approximate that first retransmission rather than later ones, which are influenced by exponential backoff. Historical round-trip data from other connections to the same host or prefix can also influence the delay.

The delay MUST have a lower bound: a subsequent connection MUST NOT be started within 10 milliseconds of the previous attempt. The recommended minimum is 100 milliseconds, the Minimum Connection Attempt Delay, and that minimum is required to avoid congestion collapse in the presence of high packet-loss rates. The delay SHOULD also have an upper bound, the Maximum Connection Attempt Delay, currently recommended as 2 seconds.

Section 8 collects the values a client may configure: the Resolution Delay at 50 milliseconds, the First Address Family Count at 1, the Connection Attempt Delay at 250 milliseconds, the Minimum Connection Attempt Delay at 100 milliseconds and the Maximum Connection Attempt Delay at 2 seconds. They were determined empirically by measuring the timing of connections on a very wide set of production devices, and were picked to reduce wait times noticed by users while minimizing load on the network. The RFC expects them to change over time as networks evolve, and welcomes implementations that use different values.
sections.plainLanguage: The client starts with one address and, if that does not connect within a short wait, starts the next one. The wait is 250 milliseconds by default, and never less than 10 milliseconds, so a network is not flooded with attempts. As soon as one attempt succeeds, the others are dropped.

sections.title: IPv6-Only Networks with NAT64 and DNS64
sections.content:
Most IPv6 transition protocols are transparent to client devices, but the combined use of NAT64 and DNS64 requires changes in client devices. One option is for the client networking stack to implement 464XLAT, which has the advantage of not requiring changes to user-space software. It does, however, require per-packet translation when an application uses IPv4 literals, and it does not encourage client application software to support native IPv6. On platforms that do not support 464XLAT, the Happy Eyeballs engine SHOULD follow this section to support IPv6-only networks properly. The features described here SHOULD only be enabled when the host detects such a network. A simple heuristic is to check whether the network offers routable IPv6 addressing, does not offer routable IPv4 addressing, and offers a DNS resolver address.

For IPv4 address literals, Section 7.1 explains that the engine performs NAT64 address synthesis. It queries the network for the NAT64 prefix using the discovery method of RFC 7050 and synthesizes an appropriate IPv6 address, or several, with the encoding of RFC 6052. The synthesized addresses are inserted into the list as if they had come from DNS queries, and connection attempts follow the same algorithm.

Section 7.2 covers hostnames that resolve to valid A records and broken AAAA records, which it defines as AAAA records that contain seemingly valid IPv6 addresses that never reply when contacted on the usual ports. The causes it lists are mistyping the IPv6 address in the DNS zone configuration, routing black holes and service outages. On IPv6-only networks with NAT64 and DNS64 such hostnames do not work, because DNS64 recursive resolvers rely on authoritative name servers sending negative responses for AAAA records in order to synthesize, and they instead pass the broken AAAA record through. The client must then query for the A record and perform local synthesis. To minimize load on DNS servers, that A query is performed only when the client has given up on the AAAA records it first received, using a longer timeout called the Last Resort Local Synthesis Delay, recommended to be 2 seconds. The timer starts when the last connection attempt is fired.

Section 7.3 covers VPNs that handle DNS queries for the device, whether for all queries or a subset such as *.internal.example.com. If an internal hostname resolves to an external IPv4 address, the client ends up with an IPv4 address and no route to it. The company's resolver cannot synthesize, because it does not know the NAT64 prefix of the underlying network, and the network's DNS64 resolver cannot resolve the hostname, because it does not know the company's internal addresses. The client must resolve the A record through the company's resolver and then synthesize an IPv6 address locally, as if the resolved IPv4 address had been provided by the application.
sections.plainLanguage: On a network with IPv6 only, a client may still need to reach IPv4 servers. The engine turns IPv4 addresses into IPv6 ones itself, using the network's NAT64 prefix, and starts the attempts as usual. It waits longer before taking that step, so that DNS servers are not loaded with extra queries.

sections.title: Limitations
sections.content:
Happy Eyeballs handles initial connection failures at the TCP/IP layer, but other failures or performance issues may still affect the connection that is chosen.

Path maximum transmission unit discovery (Section 9.1): Happy Eyeballs is only active during the initial handshake, and TCP does not pass that handshake, so issues related to the maximum transmission unit can be masked and go unnoticed during Happy Eyeballs. Solving that is out of scope; one solution is Packetization Layer Path MTU Discovery in RFC 4821.

The application layer (Section 9.2): if DNS returns multiple addresses for different application servers, the application itself may not be operational and functional on all of them. The examples given are Transport Layer Security and HTTP.

Hiding operational issues (Section 9.3): it has been observed in practice that Happy Eyeballs can hide issues in networks. If a misconfiguration causes IPv6 to consistently fail on a given network while IPv4 is still functional, Happy Eyeballs may impair the operator's ability to notice the issue. The RFC recommends that network operators deploy external means of monitoring to ensure the functionality of all address families.
sections.plainLanguage: The method only covers the first handshake. It says nothing about problems that appear later, such as a packet size that does not fit the network, or a server that answers on one address but not another. It also warns that a working IPv4 path can hide a broken IPv6 path, so operators should monitor both kinds separately.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC notes that applications should not rely on a stable mapping from hostname to address to ensure any security properties, since DNS results may change between queries. Happy Eyeballs may make it more likely that subsequent connections to a single hostname use different IP addresses.

The document requires no IANA actions.
sections.plainLanguage: Because a name can point to different addresses at different times, a program must not treat the address as part of its security check. The method makes such changes more likely, since later connections may use different addresses.

viz.caption: ILLUSTRATIVE, NOT FROM THE RFC: THE FOUR PHASES AS ONE FLOW

messages.label: AAAA query
messages.note: Sent first and immediately followed by the A query.

messages.label: AAAA response
messages.note: A positive response starts the IPv6 attempt at once.

messages.label: A response
messages.note: If this arrives first, the client waits 50 milliseconds for AAAA.

messages.label: IPv6 attempt
messages.note: Started first when the IPv6 address is preferred.

messages.label: IPv4 attempt
messages.note: Started 250 milliseconds later if the first attempt has not succeeded.

items.label: Resolution Delay
items.desc: Wait for an AAAA response after an A response arrives.

items.label: First Address Family Count
items.desc: Addresses of the first family to try before the other family; 2 may be used to favor one family more.

items.label: Connection Attempt Delay
items.desc: Wait between attempts when there is no round-trip data.

items.label: Minimum Connection Attempt Delay
items.desc: Shortest recommended wait; a subsequent attempt MUST NOT start within 10 milliseconds.

items.label: Last Resort Local Synthesis Delay
items.desc: Wait after the last attempt before sending the A query on an IPv6-only network.
